source.title: The Growth Engine
source.summary: The Solow growth model, steady states, convergence failures, and why human capital is the missing variable.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: The Solow growth model is the workhorse of growth economics. An economy produces output using capital and labor. Each year, some output is saved and invested. But capital depreciates, and diminishing returns set in. The key insight: capital accumulation alone can't sustain growth forever. Only technological progress drives long-run growth. The model predicts convergence: poor countries should grow faster. But many Muslim-majority countries haven't converged. Pakistan's per-capita growth has been anemic for decades. Indonesia did better. Malaysia succeeded. The pattern isn't about Islam. It's about institutions and governance. This episode extends the model to include human capital, where the Islamic tradition's emphasis on ilm (knowledge) should be an advantage, but modern Muslim-majority states have largely failed to translate that tradition into actual educational investment.

linkedin.post: The Solow growth model remains the workhorse of growth economics, built on a simple premise: economies produce output using capital and labor, with savings driving investment. But the model's most striking prediction—that poor countries should grow faster than rich ones due to diminishing returns—hasn't held for many Muslim-majority nations. Pakistan's per-capita growth has been anemic for decades. Indonesia performed better. Malaysia succeeded remarkably. The pattern isn't about Islamic principles but about institutions and governance. When we extend the model to include human capital, Islam's emphasis on ilm (knowledge) should theoretically provide an advantage. Yet convergence failures persist across many Muslim-majority countries, pointing to deeper structural challenges in how knowledge translates into economic growth. Listen to the full analysis: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-re-2
